title: Jaeda Yurkiw
text:
I’m Jaeda, an EIT (Engineer-in-Training) who graduated from civil engineering at UBC Okanagan this past June. During my degree, I worked in the Construction Integration and Digitalization Lab under Dr. Qian Chen.
In my fourth year, I proposed and led a capstone project called BIM-AI Smart Construction, which won first place in Software and Data Systems, an experience that sparked my interest in data science.
I’m now pursuing a Master of Data Science at UBC, and I’m excited to explore where the intersection of civil engineering and data science can take me, whether that’s in intelligent infrastructure, AI-driven systems, or something I haven’t discovered yet.

title: Life expectancy in Iran over time
text:
In this post I use R to explore how life in Iran changed between 1952 and 2007.
Data: gapminder R package by Jennifer Bryan (CC0), an excerpt of data from the Gapminder Foundation (CC BY 4.0).

title: Life expectancy in Iran over time
text:
Setup

library(gapminder)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

title: Life expectancy in Iran over time
text:
Removing missing life expentancy values

countries <- gapminder |>
    filter(!is.na(lifeExp))
head(countries)

title: Life expectancy in Iran over time
text:
Visualizing life expectancy for Iran

ggplot(iran_life_exp, aes(x = year, y = lifeExp)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Life expectancy (years)")







Figure 1: Life expectancy in Iran, 1952 to 2007.

title: Life expectancy in Iran over time
section: What I did and what I found
text:
What I did and what I found
I first removed rows with missing life expectancy values, then filtered the data to include only Iran. Next, I sorted the years by life expectancy in descending order to see the highest and lowest, and finally plotted life expectancy over time as a line chart.
Life expectancy in Iran increased steadily from 1952 to 2007. In 1952, life expectancy was around 50 years, and by 2007 it had risen to around 72 years, an increase of about 22 years (Figure 1).

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
My first few weeks in the MDS have been exciting, rewarding, and definitely challenging! I knew the program would be fast-paced, but experiencing it firsthand has been an adjustment. Orientation week was a great way to begin the program. I really enjoyed getting to know my classmates and learning more about what to expect from the year ahead.
The first few weeks of classes have been both overwhelming and challenging. Since I don’t come from a coding background, there has been a lot of new material to learn, and I’ve had to put in extra time and effort to build a strong foundation. Although it has been challenging, it has also been rewarding to see my progress. I’m learning something new every day, and I’m excited to continue building my technical skills throughout the program.
One of the things that has surprised me most about the MDS has been how supportive and encouraging the professors and program team are. Compared with my undergraduate experience, where I sometimes felt more on my own, the MDS community has made it clear that they genuinely want students to succeed and are there to support us along the way. I’m grateful to be part of the MDS program and excited to continue developing my skills, learning from my classmates and professors, and seeing where this experience takes me.

Visualizing body mass for Adelie

Figure 1: Distribution of body mass for Adelie penguins.

title: Body mass of Adelie penguin species
section: What I did and what I found
text:
What I did and what I found
I first removed rows with missing body mass values, then filtered the data to include only Adelie penguins. Next, I sorted their body masses in descending order to see the heaviest and lightest penguins, and finally plotted the distribution as a histogram.
The heaviest Adelie penguin weighs 4,775 g and the lightest weighs 2,850 g. The most common body mass range is about 3,880 to 4,000 g, which contains 18 penguins. The fewest penguins (2) weigh about 4,520 to 4,650 g. Overall, Figure 1 shows that most Adelie penguins weigh between about 3,250 g and 4,000 g.

title: About
text:
Why data science
My interest in data science and artificial intelligence grew after joining the Construction Integration and Digitalization (CID) Lab at UBC Okanagan, where I saw how these tools could solve real problems in construction and structural engineering. Through two engineering internships, I noticed how many structural workflows still relied on slow, manual processes, pushing me to look beyond traditional engineering toward integrated, data-centric systems.
This led me to propose BIM-AI Smart Construction as my capstone project with my research supervisor, which won first place in Software and Data Systems and ultimately inspired me to pursue a Master of Data Science.

title: About
text:
Outside of data science
Outside of data science, I love staying active. I’ve played high-level indoor and beach volleyball for most of my life, making it my favourite sport to play. I also enjoy road biking and running, and I love spending time outdoors with friends and family.
I’ve also always enjoyed music and started playing piano at a young age. More recently, I’ve enjoyed creating content for my engineering-focused Instagram account, where I share my experiences and interests in engineering and data science and hope to inspire young girls to pursue STEM. On weekends, I’m usually trying a new restaurant, exploring somewhere new, or spending time with friends and family.
